Harlem Renaissance. A cultural and intellectual awakening of African Americans centered in Harlem, a neighborhood of New York City, the Harlem Renaissance flourished primarily during the nineteen-twenties and nineteen-thirties. African American writers, musicians, visual artists, and intellectuals created a dynamic new culture celebrating Black identity, heritage, and artistic achievement. The movement produced literary masterpieces, revolutionary music in jazz and blues, and visual art that challenged racist stereotypes and asserted African American cultural pride, establishing the foundation for the modern Civil Rights Movement.

The Great Migration from nineteen ten to nineteen seventy brought millions of African Americans from the rural South to northern industrial cities. Harlem emerged as the largest African American community, creating a critical mass of talented artists and intellectuals.

Langston Hughes became the movement's poetic voice, celebrating African American vernacular, jazz rhythms, and folk traditions in poetry that was both intellectually sophisticated and accessible to ordinary people. Zora Neale Hurston, an anthropologist and writer, collected African American folklore and produced novels celebrating Black Southern rural culture and female independence, most famously Their Eyes Were Watching God in nineteen thirty-seven. Claude McKay, Countee Cullen, James Weldon Johnson, and Jessie Faucet produced poetry and prose exploring African American identity and the complexities of living under Jim Crow segregation.

Duke Ellington and Louis Armstrong revolutionized music. Jazz became the defining musical form of the era, blending African American blues, ragtime, and improvisation into an art form that conquered American and eventually world culture.

The Cotton Club epitomized the era's contradictions: a nightclub featuring African American musicians and dancers, yet owned by white entrepreneurs and restricted to white patrons. The movement championed the New Negro, asserting African American agency, dignity, and cultural achievement. Arts salons and intellectual gatherings, often hosted by wealthy white patrons in a phenomenon called the Negro vogue, created spaces for cultural exchange, though on unequal terms reflecting broader white control.

The Harlem Renaissance produced visual art and sculpture celebrating African and African American aesthetics, drawing on modernist styles while asserting cultural authenticity and pride. These artists and intellectuals established a legacy whose ideology and consciousness directly shaped the Civil Rights Movement decades later, asserting that Black pride and dignity were foundational to American culture.
